CNV.name: Choroidal neovascularisation (wet AMD)
CNV.what_it_is: Abnormal blood vessels growing at the back of the eye, which is the cause of wet age-related macular degeneration. It is less common than the dry form but can worsen quickly, sometimes within days or weeks.
common_symptoms: difficulty seeing fine detail such as small print
straight lines appearing wavy or distorted
gaps or dark spots in central vision
typical_next_steps: See an optometrist straight away if you notice distortion or sudden changes in central vision
If wet AMD is suspected, you may be referred to an eye doctor (ophthalmologist) or specialist AMD service, usually within about a week
Treatment can help stop vision getting worse, and wet AMD can often be treated if caught early
self_care: Use an Amsler grid regularly to check each eye separately; contact your eye-care professional straight away if the lines look wavy, broken or missing
Stop smoking if you smoke, which is the single most effective step for eye health
Eat a balanced diet including plenty of fresh fruit and dark green leafy vegetables
Keep blood pressure and cholesterol under control, as both are linked to AMD
Protect your eyes from UV light with sunglasses
Ask your eye-care professional whether supplements are appropriate for you rather than starting them yourself
CNV.source: NHS AMD getting diagnosed (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/age-related-macular-degeneration-amd/getting-diagnosed/); NHS Wales Eye Care, Lifestyle and eye health (https://www.nhs.wales/sa/eye-care-wales/)

DME.name: Diabetic macular oedema
DME.what_it_is: A form of diabetic retinopathy in which fluid leaks and collects in the macula, the central part of the retina, causing it to swell. It affects central vision while peripheral vision is usually unaffected.
typical_next_steps: Attend your annual diabetic eye screening appointment, which is designed to catch this early
Visit your optician regularly and tell the optometrist that you are diabetic
Treatments are available; a specialist will discuss the options with you
self_care: Keep blood sugar levels within the range agreed with your diabetes care team, and monitor them regularly
Keep blood pressure and cholesterol under control, as both affect how quickly retinopathy progresses
Stop smoking if you smoke; smoking substantially accelerates damage to the eyes
Eat a healthy, balanced diet, cutting down on salt, fat and sugar
Attend every diabetic eye screening appointment, even if your diabetes feels well controlled
Get professional advice straight away if you notice any new problem with your sight
DME.source: NHS Diabetic retinopathy prevention (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/diabetic-retinopathy/prevention); York and Scarborough Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, Diabetic eye screening (https://www.yorkhospitals.nhs.uk/)

DRUSEN.name: Drusen
DRUSEN.what_it_is: Small deposits of lipid and protein under the retina, visible as yellow dots. Drusen can be a normal part of ageing, but medium or large drusen at the macula can indicate early age-related macular degeneration.
common_symptoms: often none in the early stages
typical_next_steps: Drusen are commonly picked up during a routine eye examination by an optometrist
Early and intermediate AMD may cause no vision loss and no symptoms, so regular eye tests matter
See an optometrist straight away if straight lines start to look wavy or distorted, which can indicate the wet form developing
self_care: Have regular eye examinations, including a check of the macula
Use an Amsler grid to check each eye, and report any distortion promptly
Stop smoking if you smoke
Eat a diet with plenty of fresh fruit and dark green leafy vegetables
Keep blood pressure and cholesterol under control
Wear sunglasses to protect against UV light
DRUSEN.source: RNIB Age-related macular degeneration (https://www.rnib.org.uk/your-eyes/amd-awareness-month/more-information-on-amd/); NHS Wales Eye Care, Lifestyle and eye health (https://www.nhs.wales/sa/eye-care-wales/)

NORMAL.name: Normal retina
NORMAL.what_it_is: This scan did not show features the system associates with the three retinal conditions it was trained on.
typical_next_steps: A 'normal' result does not rule out eye disease; this system was trained on only three conditions
See an optometrist if you notice any changes in your vision, particularly distortion of straight lines or difficulty seeing detail
If you have diabetes, continue attending your annual diabetic eye screening regardless of this result
self_care: Have a regular eye examination; an eye test should be part of everyone's routine health care
Stop smoking if you smoke, which benefits eye health as well as general health
Keep blood pressure and cholesterol under control
Wear sunglasses in strong sunlight
See an optometrist promptly about any new change in your vision, rather than waiting for your next routine test
NORMAL.source: NHS Wales Eye Care, Lifestyle and eye health (https://www.nhs.wales/sa/eye-care-wales/); NHS AMD getting diagnosed (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/age-related-macular-degeneration-amd/getting-diagnosed/)
